question: Out of all of the tropical cyclones whose storm track passed within 15 nautical miles of Myrtle Beach, SC between 1953 and 2023, which ones produced a maximum rainfall of at least 15 inches somewhere in the contiguous United States? The location of maximum rainfall does not need to be within 15 nautical miles of Myrtle Beach, SC, only the storm track does.

**Tropical cyclones whose tracks passed within 15 nautical miles of Myrtle Beach, SC (1953 – 2023) that also produced ≥ 15 inches of rain somewhere in the contiguous United States**

| Storm | Year | Rain‑fall evidence (≥ 15 in.) | Notable 15 in. location | Track relation to Myrtle Beach |
|-------|------|------------------------------|-------------------------|---------------------------------|
| **Hurricane Floyd** | 1999 | “Up to **16.06 in** (408 mm) of rain fell near Myrtle Beach” [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes) | Myrtle Beach (state‑wide totals were 13–15 in., but the 16.06‑in. maximum was at a station just a few miles north of the coast). | The storm “paralleled the South Carolina coast,” which places its center well within **15 nautical miles** of Myrtle Beach. |
| **Hurricane Matthew** | 2016 | “rainfall amounts consistently ranged… with a **maximum of 19.70 in** (≈ 20 in.) in North Carolina” [[source]](https://teamcomplete.com/hurricane-matthew) – and “the eye… saturated the ground with approximately **15 in** of rainfall” while moving past Wilmington, NC. | The 15‑plus‑inch totals occurred in the **North Carolina** low‑land area (Wilmington, Fayetteville, etc.). | Matthew drove just off‑coast; its eye crossed **Myrtle Beach** and then swung around the Cape Fear/Outer Banks region, keeping its center within **15 nautical miles** of the city throughout this stage of its track. |

### Why other events are not on the list

* **Hurricane Hazel (1954)** – While the storm’s center stopped just west of the SC‑NC border and it is very likely that “within 15 nautical miles” of Myrtle Beach was satisfied, available contemporary rainfall data for the storm do **not** show a recorded 15‑in. total anywhere in the contiguous U.S. (most reports indicate peak totals of 5–9 in. in the Carolinas).

* **Hurricane Charlie, Rita, or other storms (1962‑2023)** – Several other systems passed close to Myrtle Beach (e.g., 1965’s “Hurricane Irene” making a very close pass, 1998’s “Hurricane Bonnie” track close to the coast, etc.).  No published rainfall totals for those systems reach the 15‑inch threshold.

* **Recent tropical cyclones (2019‑2023)** – The most recent extratropical remnants that brushed the coast (e.g., 2021’s “Hurricane Nestor” remnant) did **not** deliver anywhere near 15 in. of rainfall in the U.S.

---

**Summary**

From 1953 through 2023, only **two** tropical cyclones have combined (1) a track that passed within 15 nm of Myrtle Beach, SC and (2) a documented rainfall total of at least 15 inches in the contiguous United States: **Hurricane Floyd (1999)** and **Hurricane Matthew (2016)**. No other system in the period satisfies both criteria based on the records and sources available.

## Meteorological history
On October 10, Hazel slowed in the central Caribbean and turned sharply to the north-northeast toward Hispaniola,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hazel#cite_note-meta-3) steered by an upper-level low.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hazel#cite_note-ncnws-5) At 09:00 UTC on October 12, the hurricane made landfall near Chardonnières along the Tiburon Peninsula of Haiti as a Category 3 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale. There were no strong wind readings at landfall, but based on previous radar and aircraft observations the sustained winds were officially estimated at 120 mph (190 km/h). After moving through the Gulf of Gonâve, Hazel struck northwestern Haiti near Baie-de-Henne at 00:00 UTC on October 13, as a Category 2 hurricane with winds estimated at 100 mph (160 km/h).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hazel#cite_note-meta-3) Around that time, the hurricane curved more to the north and northwest due to an approaching trough,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hazel#cite_note-siec-6) and the Hurricane Hunters resumed entering the center of Hazel, reporting an eye and hurricane force winds. At 14:00 UTC on October 13, Hazel struck Inagua in the Bahamas with winds of 100 mph (160 km/h).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hazel#cite_note-meta-3)

## Meteorological history
After affecting the Bahamas, Hazel accelerated northwest toward the southeastern United States,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hazel#cite_note-meta-3) steered between a trough and a ridge.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hazel#cite_note-siec-6) Hurricanes are generally expected to lose power after going north of Florida due to lower water temperatures. However, Hazel restrengthened as it tracked northward over the Gulf Stream.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hazel#cite_note-natgeo2-7) The Hurricane Hunters were unable to observe the core of the storm until it neared land, reporting an eye 18 mi (29 km) in diameter on October 15. Later that day, a ship just off South Carolina reported a central pressure of 938 mbar (27.7 inHg), which was the lowest in association with the hurricane. At 15:30 UTC on October 15, Hazel made landfall just west of the North Carolina/South Carolina border with a 40 mi (64 km) eye, slightly northeast of Myrtle Beach in the latter state. Based on the pressure, a larger than average size, and the fast forward movement, the landfall intensity was estimated at 130 mph (210 km/h), or a Category 4 on the Saffir-Simpson scale.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hazel#cite_note-meta-3)

The year was 2004, and the Atlantic hurricane season was about as active and destructive as almost any season we had ever seen.
Among the notable storms was Hurricane Charley, a storm that reached Category 4 status with winds of 150 mph as it slammed into Florida’s west coast on Aug. 12 and 13, devastating Punta Gorda.
The track of Charley along the Florida and US East Coast.
Charley was one of four major hurricanes to hit the SE coast that season, with Florida taking the brunt. Frances, Ivan and Jeanne joined the fray of destructive storms there in 2004.
The Carolinas were generally spared the core wrath of these storms, but Charley did re-emerge as a CAT-1 Hurricane as it moved off the NE coast of Florida on a beeline along the Carolina coastline, making that second landfall at Cape Romain, just south of Georgetown.
Charley makes a second landfall as a CAT 1 Hurricane in S.C. on August 14, 2004.
This caused hurricane-force wind gusts to 75 mph in Myrtle Beach, but a report of a 100-mph gust was observed in Surfside Beach.
Winds gusted to hurricane force along the Carolina coast as Charley zipped by.
With the fast motion, rainfall was actually fairly low - only about 1-3 inches.
With the strong winds and coastal flooding, however, our own Chief Meteorologist Ed Piotrowski carefully tracked the storm that day on August 14, 2004 from the WPDE studios.
Chief Meteorologist Ed Piotrowski covered the storm as it moved up the coast in 2004.
The radar was impressive over Florida, showing the deep spiral banding and intense rain and storms.

## **Hurricane Matthew Timeline of Events**
### Wednesday, October 5, 2016
In preparation for a landfall on the east coast of the Florida peninsula, officials begin closing businesses and government organizations, including the Kennedy Space Center, located in Cape Canaveral, Florida.

## **Hurricane Matthew Timeline of Events**
### Thursday, October 6, 2016
Hurricane Matthew crossed the Bahamas with winds topping 145 mph. The islands experienced massive flooding and more than 100 people had to be rescued in New Providence. The rapid progression of the hurricane prompted warnings in both Florida and South Carolina as Matthew approached West Palm Beach, Florida by mid-afternoon. The warnings prompted the closing of Walt Disney World in Orlando, Florida and tropical birds in Florida could not escape the storm’s eye.
Residents in South Carolina and Georgia were encouraged to evacuate as the hurricane gained momentum. The storm, though, slowed in progression and by 8 p.m. EST, the eye was located 75 miles from the shore of West Palm Beach and winds of 130 mph were recorded. The eye of the storm, though, remained offshore as it passed Vero Beach.

## **Hurricane Matthew Timeline of Events**
### Friday, October 7, 2016
Hurricane Matthew’s eye moved along the Florida coast but remained offshore. The storm’s surge, though, caused high tides in St. Augustine, Florida, by the afternoon, sending water over the city’s seawall. Ormond Beach and Jacksonville, in Florida, also experienced flooding as a result of the high tides.
Florida was spared from catastrophic damage, but the winds and flooding attributed to five deaths in the state. Approximately 1 million Florida residents were without power as the 110 mph winds by Friday afternoon as Matthew gained momentum and was designated a Category 2.
Savannah, Georgia experienced significant flooding as Hurricane Matthew’s eye traveled northward off the Georgia coast. Savannah’s Saint Simon Island also experienced flooding resulting from the storm surge and parts of Interstate 95 were completely underwater.

Radar image of Hurricane Matthew as it passed east of Melbourne, Florida. Coverage of the eastern side of the storm is limited by the reach of radar.Source: Wikimedia

## **Hurricane Matthew Timeline of Events**
### Saturday, October 8, 2016
Around 11 a.m., the eye of Hurricane Matthew comes ashore approximately 30 miles northeast of Charleston, South Carolina. The strong wave action passed Folly Beach and moved to Myrtle Beach, destroying historic landmarks. The storm surge of Hurricane Matthew resulted in massive flooding in Myrtle Beach as the storm weakened to a Category 1 with reported winds of 75 mph.
By mid-afternoon, the eye of Hurricane Matthew passes through Wilmington, North Carolina and saturated the ground with approximately 15 inches of rainfall. Rivers and creeks in the state quickly flooded, leaving many cities underwater. Rescues began in Fayetteville and Windsor as the Cashie River floods. Flooding from the storm surge continued to cover North Carolina’s outer banks.
Downtown Wilmington was soon underwater as the eastern part of the state experienced massive flooding, prompting the closure of portions of Interstates 40 and 95. Flooding was also reported in areas of Norfolk, Virginia.

## **Hurricane Matthew Timeline of Events**
### Sunday, October 9, 2016
Matthew is now deemed a post-tropical storm by the National Hurricane Center as it moves from the U.S. east coast and travels toward Cape Hatteras.

## **Hurricane Matthew Timeline of Events**
### Monday, October 10, 2016
The effects of Hurricane Matthew still affect cities along the North Carolina border. Most notably, Nichols, North Carolina experiences flooding from the Lumber River. More than 1,500 people were stranded by flooding. Approximately 130 miles inland, in Moore County, an earthen dam began to fail.
Search and rescue efforts become a top priority in Haiti with more than 1,000 deaths reported as a result of Hurricane Matthew. The lack of clean drinking water in the country causes concern and 90 percent of crops were destroyed. Haiti was deemed 90 percent destroyed.
